JUDGMENT:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused no.1 (since expired) is stated to be the vendor-cum-partner of accused no. 4 firm M/s.

sentences.text: Kanwarji Bhagirath Mal, of which accused no. 2 and 3 were also the partners, from where the food article, that is, 'Laddu' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 07.11.2001, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Arun Kumar and Sanjeev Gupta under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Arun Mishra reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Kanwarji Bhagirath Mal, at 1972,
Chandni Chowk, Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Laddus from the vendor, to which he had agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 15.11.2001, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that total dye content of the synthetic colour used was 503.45 ppm which was exceeding the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
It was revealed that the accused no. 4 was a partnership firm of which accused no. 1,2 and 3 were the partners in charge of and responsible to the firm for its business.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 13.12.2002 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 13.12.2002.

The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 28.02.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rues due to presence of dye content upto 670.5 ppm which is more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm as per Rule 30 of PFA Rules.
4. The matter was listed for pre-charge evidence wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Virender Singh and PW-2 FI Arun Kumar.

Based on their deposition, vide order dated 05.12.2009 (the charge mentions the date as 04.12.2009), charge was framed against accused no. 2,3 and 4 (accused no. 1 having already expired) for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b)(j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

Subsequently, the witnesses already examined in pre-charge stage were recalled for further cross examination in post charge stage and additionally, the complainant examined PW-3 Sh. Arun Mishra and PW-4 FI Sanjeev Kumar Gupta in post charge evidence.
It is to be noted that accused no. 1 and 2 have already expired and vide order dated 16.02.2004, accused no. 4 firm has already been discharged.
Thus, the trial in this case has been faced only by accused no.3.

sentences.text: PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 07.11.2001 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Laddus,
breaking the same into smallest pieces with the help of clean and dry spoon in a clean and dry tray and then mixing/homogenizing it, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles,
putting 40 drops of formalin in each bottle, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-2/A, notice Ex. PW-2/B, Panchnama Ex. PW- 2/C, PA Receipt Ex.
PW-2/D and LHA receipt Ex. PW-2/E.
PA report Ex. PW-2/F was received and investigation was carried out by PW-2 who sent letter Ex. PW-2/G and Ex. PW-2/H to the STO and Vendor respectively and received their replies.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/A was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/B was filed in the court by PW-1.

A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/C was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex.
PW-1/D.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.
6. Statement of the accused no. 3 under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 05.06.2013 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
He stated that he had no knowledge about the sampling proceedings as he was not present at the spot at that time.
He further claimed that he was not incharge or responsible to the firm for its business.
He chose not to lead evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.3 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 28.02.2003 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.
He has relied upon the various judgements in his support.
He further submits that there is nothing on record to show that accused no. 3 was the person incharge of or responsible to the firm for conduct of its business affairs.
It is argued that when the firm itself has been discharged, none of its partners could be prosecuted under vicarious liability.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. In a criminal case, the burden is only on the prosecution to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt by leading positive evidence.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and it has to be necessary discharged by the prosecution itself.

sentences.text: It is to be seen that the complaint was filed against accused no. 4 partnership firm as well as its three partners on the ground that they all were in charge of and responsible to the firm for its business affairs.
As already stated, two of the said partners have already expired and only third partner Roop Narain has faced the trial.

At the same time, it is seen that the accused no. 4 firm has already been discharged vide order dated 16.02.2004 relying upon the judgement titled as Assistant Commissioner, Assessment-II, Banglore v. M/s Velliappa Textiles Limited [2003 RCR (Criminal)
695 SC].

sentences.text: Needless to say, the said order has attained finality as it has never been challenged by the prosecution / complainant.

12. The question at this stage would therefore be whether the present complaint can proceed and accused no. 3 could be convicted in the capacity of a partner of firm which has already been discharged by the court and such order having attained finality.
13. Earlier, there were divergent views of various Hon'ble Courts as to if a criminal complaint is maintainable against the director of a company without implicating the company as an accused.

However, the law has been now settled by the authoritative judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India titled as Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Travels Pvt. Ltd. [(2012) 5 SCC 661].
In the said precedent

entities.text: Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Travels Pvt. Ltd. [(2012) 5 SCC 661]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , with pertains to the interpretation of section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of other persons and therefore, it is absolutely clear that only when a company can be prosecuted that the persons mentioned in other categories could be held vicariously liable for the offence committed by the company.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India overruled the previous judgements titled as Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352] and Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1] and reiterated the law as laid down in State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491].

entities.text: Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Upon going through the law so laid down, it is clear that the prime liability is on the company and it is only when the court comes to conclusion that an offence has been committed by a company that it can proceed to attribute vicarious liability to other persons who are proved to be in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs.

In the absence of the company as an accused,
the other persons including directors / shareholders / employees cannot be prosecuted independently.

14. The language of section 17 of PFA Act is pari materia to section 141 of NI Act, with respect to the role and responsibility of the persons who can be arrayed as an accused in addition to the company itself.

Like section 141 NI Act, even section 17 of PFA Act provides that in addition to the company,
any person who was in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs can also be implicated as an accused.
Further, as per Explanation (a), a company includes a firm or any association tof individuals and as per Explanation (b), a director in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm.

Thus, like section 141 NI Act, the provisions of section 17 of PFA Act would be equally applicable in case of a partnership firm as in case of a company, despite the fact that a partnership firm is not otherwise a separate legal entity as in case of a corporation.
As such, the partners in a partnership firm hold similar position as directors in a company, as far as the section 17 of PFA Act and section 141 NI Act are concerned.

At the same time, it is to be noted that to attribute vicarious liability on any director or a partner,
mere bald averments in the complaint would not be sufficient and specific role has to be attributed to that director / partner as to how such person has been said to be in charge of or responsible to the company / firm for conduct of its affairs.

Reliance can be placed on the judgement titled as SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla [(2005) 8 SCC 89] that pertains to NI Act, as well as the judgements titled as Raghav Gupta v. Food Inspector [Crl. MC No. 1488/2011, Delhi High Court,
dated 30.01.2012] and Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi [(1983) 1 SCC 1] that pertain to PFA Act.

sentences.text: It has been laid down that that mere averment that an accused being director or partner would 'as such' be liable for the acts of the company/firm would not be sufficient.

16. On the touchstone of the above discussed proportions of law, the court has to see if the accused no. 3 herein can be held liable for the offence allegedly committed by the accused no. 4 firm that has already been discharged by the court.
17. A perusal of the complaint as well as the deposition of the witnesses would show that the only allegation against the accused no. 3 is that he was a partner of accused no. 4 firm.

Other than this,
there is nothing on record to how as to how accused no. 3 has been claimed to be a person in charge of or responsible to the firm for its affairs.
As admitted by PW-2 and PW-4, only accused no. 1 (since expired) was found present at the shop on the day of lifting of sample.
Accused no. 3 was not present there or found vending any food article.

Though PW-2 during his cross examination stated that he had met all the three partners at the shop subsequently during the investigation, yet mere such presence on any other day would not be sufficient to attribute vicarious liability on all the partners.

18. A copy of the partnership deed had also been taken by the FI which only shows the profit-loss sharing ratio between the partners and other terms and conditions governing the partnership, but there is nothing even in this deed to show as to which of the three partners or otherwise all of the said partners would be having effective role and responsibility in conduct of business affairs of the firm.

The FI did not take any steps subsequently to check and seize the account books or bank records or bill books, to ascertain as to which of these partners was in charge of or responsible for day to day affairs of the firm.
No document had been collected and placed on record to show if the accused no. 3 had ever participated in any of the day to day activities of the firm.

There is nothing to show if any bills were signed by him or any orders were placed by him or if he had sold any article to any customer or purchased any article from supplier or had maintained accounts or had discharged any other routine liability of the firm.

In the absence of any such record, all the partners could not have been implicated for the offence committed by the firm, merely on the averment that being partners as such, they were in charge of or responsible to the firm for its affairs.
The material is insufficient on this count.
19. Even otherwise, since the firm itself has already been discharged and such order has already attained finality, no vicarious liability can be fastened on its partners.

It would be a very anomolous situation to say that the firm on which the principal liability would be there has already been discharged but its partners on whom only a secondary or vicarious liability is attributable has been held guilty.
As clarified in the above mentioned precedents, no conviction of any director / partner can be maintained in the absence of conviction of the company / firm itself.

But when no such Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Laxmi Narain on 18 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153914417/
5 liability can be fastened to the firm which has already been discharged by the court, no vicarious liability can be attributed even to its partner.

sentences.text: It is not a case where a firm could not be implicated on account of some technical defect or some legal incapacity.
Rather the firm has been discharged by a judicial order which has attained finality and never challenged.

In view of this position, no criminal activity can be fastened on accused no. 3.
20.

The judgments relied upon by the accused, that is, State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal [1998 AIPFA Journal 269], MCD v. Kishan Chand [1975 PFA Cases 347], MCD v. Des Raj [1984(II) PFA Cases 163], Chander Bhan v. State [1975 PFA Cases 77], and State v. Naresh Kumar [1980(II) PFA Cases 3] also go in his favour.

21. In view of this, it can be said that the complainant has not been able to establish that accused no.
3 was in charge of or responsible to the firm for conduct if its business affairs so as to attribute liability on him.

He is entitled to be given benefit of doubt.
22.
Having said so, accused no. 3 stands acquitted of the charges.

However, his bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A. CrPC.
23.
